summary: Adds simple extensions to the Link Management Protocol so neighboring label-switching routers can confirm the status of data channels. This helps find stranded resources and triggers notifications when something does not match. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary:
Some links are not plain fibre. A link may be built from separate channels, such as a timeslot in a SONET system or a wavelength, and each router at either end keeps its own view of which channels are in use.

When those views disagree, a channel looks busy on one side and free on the other, so nobody can use it and a path setup fails. This RFC adds a short exchange to the Link Management Protocol so two neighbouring routers can compare their lists and tell the management system which channels disagree.

questions: how to find stranded resources in gmpls
what is lmp data channel status confirmation
what are stranded resources in gmpls
subtitle: A way for neighbouring routers to check that they agree on which data channels are in use.

tldr.problem: In a GMPLS network the two ends of a link can disagree about whether a data channel, such as a timeslot or a wavelength, is free. The channel then looks occupied at one end and free at the other, so it cannot be used, and the operators cannot tell which channel is at fault.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds three messages to the Link Management Protocol so adjacent routers can exchange the status of the data channels they care about and compare them. A new subobject carries the status bits and the channel identifier.
tldr.outcome: A mismatched channel can be found and reported to the management plane instead of being discovered one failed path setup at a time. The RFC was later updated by RFC 6898.

today: RFC 5818 is a Proposed Standard that has not been obsoleted, and it was updated by RFC 6898, which adds LMP behaviour negotiation and configuration modifications.

sections.title: The Problem with Data Channels
sections.content:
Generalized Multiprotocol Label Switching networks are constructed from Traffic Engineering links connecting Label Switching Routers. The TE links are constructed from a set of data channels, and in this context a data channel corresponds to a resource label in a non-packet technology, such as a timeslot or a lambda.

A data channel status mismatch exists if the LSR at one end of a TE link believes the data channel is assigned to carry data, but the LSR at the other end does not. The term ready to carry data means cross-connected or bound to an end-point for the receipt or delivery of data.

Data channel mismatches cannot be detected from the TE information advertised by the routing protocols. The existence of some problems may be detected by a mismatch in the advertised bandwidths where bidirectional TE links and bidirectional services are in use, but where unidirectional services exist, or where multiple data channel mismatches occur, it is not possible to detect such errors through the routing protocol-advertised TE information. In any case there is no mechanism to isolate the mismatches by determining which data channels are at fault.

If a data channel mismatch exists, any attempt to use the data channel for a new Label Switched Path will fail. One end of the TE link may attempt to assign the TE link for use, but the other end will report the data channel as unavailable when the control plane or management plane attempts to assign it to an LSP.

Although such a situation can be resolved through the use of the Acceptable Label Set object in GMPLS signalling, that procedure is inefficient since it may require an additional signalling exchange for each LSP that is set up. When many LSPs are to be set up, and when there are many data channel mismatches, such inefficiencies become significant. It is desirable to avoid the additional signalling overhead, and to report the problems to the management plane so that they can be resolved.

Resources that are in a mismatched state are often described as stranded resources. They are not in use for any LSP, but they cannot be assigned for use by a new LSP because they appear to be in use. Although it is theoretically possible for management plane applications to audit all network resources to locate stranded resources and release them, this process is rarely performed because of the difficulty of coordinating different Element Management Systems and the associated risks of accidentally releasing in-use resources. It is therefore desirable to have a control plane mechanism that detects and reports stranded resources.
sections.plainLanguage: A channel that one router thinks is free and the other thinks is busy is wasted: nobody can put a path over it. Finding those channels by trying to set up paths wastes signalling, and auditing every resource by hand is risky, so the RFC asks the two routers to just compare notes.

sections.title: How a Mismatch Arises
sections.content:
The document describes three scenarios, each of which leaves a specific channel resource of a data link unavailable and wasted, and each of which may reduce the chance of successfully establishing an LSP. It is therefore desirable to confirm the data channel statuses as early as possible.

A mismatch caused by manual configuration. The operator may have configured a cross-connect at only one end of a TE link using an EMS. The resource at one end of the data channel is allocated, but the corresponding resource is still available at the other end. The data channel then appears available for use by the control plane when viewed from one end, and is considered unavailable from the other. Alternatively, the available end may be cross-connected by the management plane, and a misconnection may result from the other end already being cross-connected.

A mismatch caused by LSP deletion. The channel status of a data link may become mismatched during the LSP deletion process. If that process is aborted in the middle, perhaps because of a temporary control plane failure, the cross-connect at the upstream node may be removed while the downstream node still keeps its cross-connect. In the example given, an LSP traverses nodes A, B and C, and node B resets abnormally while the LSP is being deleted. The cross-connects of A and C are removed, but B's is still in use, so the statuses between A and B and between B and C are both mismatched.

Soft state mechanisms were defined in RSVP and RSVP-TE to prevent state discrepancies between LSRs, and RSVP-TE restart processes allow adjacent LSRs to resynchronise their control plane state to reinstate information about LSPs that have persisted in the data plane. Both aim at keeping state consistency among nodes. Data channel mismatches may arise after a restart and might not be cleared up by the restart procedures.

Failed resources. It might happen that a termination point of a TE link is seen as failed by one end while on the other end it is seen as OK, owing to a failure in the hardware or in the status detection of the termination point. In that case the upstream node chooses to use the termination point in order to receive traffic from the downstream node. From the upstream node's point of view the resource is available and usable, but in the downstream node the corresponding termination point is broken, which leads to a setup failure.
sections.plainLanguage: Three things cause the disagreement: someone cross-connected one end by hand, a path teardown that stopped half way, or a piece of hardware that one end thinks is broken and the other does not.

sections.title: Why This Is an Operational Concern
sections.content:
The requirement does not come from a lack in the GMPLS specifications themselves but rather from operational concerns, because in most cases GMPLS-controlled networks will co-exist with legacy networks and legacy procedures.

The protocol extensions defined in the document are intended to detect data plane problems resulting from misuse or misconfigurations triggered by user error, or resulting from failure to clean up the data plane after control plane disconnection. It is anticipated that human mistakes are probably the major source of errors to deal with. The document is not intended to provide a protocol mechanism to deal with broken implementations.

The procedures are designed to be performed on a periodic or on-demand basis. It is NOT RECOMMENDED that the procedures be used to provide a continuous and on-line monitoring process. As LMP is already used to verify data plane connectivity, it is considered an appropriate candidate to support this feature.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a tool for operators, not a continuous monitoring system. Run it when something looks wrong or on a schedule, not as a permanent check.

sections.title: The Three New LMP Messages
sections.content:
The new LMP messages are sent between adjacent nodes periodically or driven by some event, such as an operator command, a configurable timer, or the rejection of an LSP setup message because of an unavailable resource. They run over the control channel, encapsulated in UDP with an LMP port number and IP addressing as defined in the Link Management Protocol specification.

The ConfirmDataChannelStatus message provides the remote end of the data channel with the status of the local end and asks the remote end to report its data channel. It may report on and request information about more than one data channel. Its encoding is a common header, a LOCAL_LINK_ID, a MESSAGE_ID and one or more DATA_LINK objects. When a node receives it, and the data channel status confirmation procedure is supported, the node compares its own data channel statuses with all of the statuses sent by the remote end. If a mismatch is found, the mismatch result is expected to be reported to the management plane for further action. Management plane reporting procedures and actions are outside the scope of the document. If the MESSAGE_ID value is less than the largest MESSAGE_ID previously received from the sender for the specified TE link, the message SHOULD be treated as being out-of-order.

The ConfirmDataChannelStatusAck message is sent back to the node that originated the request to return the requested data channel statuses. Its encoding is a common header, a MESSAGE_ID_ACK and one or more DATA_LINK objects, and the contents of the MESSAGE_ID_ACK objects MUST be obtained from the ConfirmDataChannelStatus message being acknowledged. When it is received, the node compares the received remote statuses with the local ones, and a mismatch is expected to be reported to the management plane. This message is used both when the data channel statuses match and when they do not.

The ConfirmDataChannelStatusNack message is sent when the confirmation procedure is not supported but the message is recognized, in which case it carries an ERROR_CODE indicating that the channel status confirmation procedure is not supported. If the procedure is supported but the node is unable to begin it, the message carries an ERROR_CODE indicating that it is unwilling to confirm. On receiving such a message, the originator MAY schedule retransmission of the ConfirmDataChannelStatus message after a configured time, and a default value of 10 minutes is suggested for that timer. Its encoding is a common header, an optional LOCAL_LINK_ID, a MESSAGE_ID_ACK and an ERROR_CODE. The ERROR_CODE object has a new class type but is formed as the ERROR_CODE object defined in the Link Management Protocol specification. Two error codes are defined: 0x01 for channel status confirmation procedure not supported, and 0x02 for unwilling to confirm.
sections.plainLanguage: Three new message types: a request that carries the sender's own view of the channels, an answer that carries the other side's view, and a refusal that says why no answer is coming. The refusal carries a code, and the sender is advised to retry about ten minutes later.

sections.title: The Data Channel Status Subobject
sections.content:
A new Data Channel Status subobject type is introduced to the DATA_LINK object to hold the Data Channel Status and Data Channel ID. The subobject carries a type and a length, then the Data Channel Status, which is a series of bit flags, and then the Data Channel ID.

Two values of the Data Channel Status are defined: 0x0000 means the channel is available or free, and 0x0001 means the channel is unavailable or in use.

The Data Channel ID identifies the data channel. The length of this field can be deduced from the Length field in the subobject. All subobjects must be padded to a four-byte boundary with trailing zeros, and if such padding is required the Length field MUST indicate the length of the subobject up to, but not including, the first byte of padding, so the amount of padding is deduced and not represented in the Length field. The Data Channel ID is given in the context of the sender of the message.

The Data Channel ID must be encoded as a label value. Based on the type of signal, such as SONET/SDH or Lambda, the encoding methodology used will be different; for SONET/SDH the label value is encoded as specified in RFC 4606.

Message construction follows the existing LMP rules. The Data_Link class is included in the ConfirmDataChannelStatus and ConfirmDataChannelStatusAck messages. The status of the TE link end MUST be carried by the Data Channel Status subobject, and the new subobject MUST be part of the Data_Link class. In the case of SONET/SDH, the Data Channel ID SHOULD be used to identify each timeslot of the data link.
sections.plainLanguage: Each channel is described by a small record: a status of free or in use, plus an identifier for the channel written the way that signalling system names its resources. The record is padded to a four-byte boundary, and the length field tells the receiver where the real data ends.

sections.title: How the Confirmation Runs
sections.content:
Adjacent nodes MAY send data channel status confirmation-related LMP messages. Periodical timers or other events may trigger these messages, and it is a local policy decision to start the process.

Initially, the sender constructs a ConfirmDataChannelStatus message that MUST contain one or more DATA_LINK objects. Each DATA_LINK object MUST contain one or more Data Channel Status subobjects, and the Data Channel ID field MUST indicate which data channel needs to be confirmed and MUST report the data channel status at the sender. The message is sent to the receiver.

Upon receipt of a ConfirmDataChannelStatus message, the receiver MUST extract the data channel statuses from it and SHOULD compare these with its own statuses for the reported data channels. If a mismatch is found, the mismatch result SHOULD be reported to the management plane for further action. The receiver also SHOULD send the ConfirmDataChannelStatusAck message, which MUST carry all the local end statuses of the requested data channels.

If the receiver is not able to support or begin the confirmation procedure, it MUST send a ConfirmDataChannelStatusNack message containing the ERROR_CODE that indicates the reason for rejection. Upon receipt of a ConfirmDataChannelStatusAck message, the sender MUST compare the received remote statuses with the local ones, and a mismatch SHOULD be reported to the management plane.

The data channel status mismatch issue identified by LMP may be automatically resolved by RSVP restart. For example, the restarting node may also have damaged its data plane, which leaves the data channels mismatched, but RSVP restart will re-install the data plane state in the restarting node. The issue may also be resolved via RSVP soft state timeout.

If the ConfirmDataChannelStatus message is not recognized by the receiver, the receiver ignores it and sends no acknowledgment. Due to message loss, the sender may not receive the acknowledgment. ConfirmDataChannelStatus SHOULD be sent using the LMP reliable transmission mechanisms. If, after the retry limit is reached, neither an acknowledgment nor a rejection is received, the sender SHOULD terminate the data channel confirmation procedure and SHOULD raise an alert to the management plane.

The document also notes that the behaviour of an LMP node that receives an unknown message is not specified in the Link Management Protocol document and will be clarified separately. Since the behaviour of legacy nodes must be assumed to be unknown, the document assumes that a deployment intended to support this function will consist completely of nodes that support the protocol extensions described in it.
sections.plainLanguage: One router sends its list, the other replies with its list, and each side compares them with what it already had. A disagreement is passed to the management system. If the reply never arrives, the procedure stops and an alert is raised rather than being retried forever.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The Link Management Protocol specification describes how LMP messages between peers can be secured, and those measures are equally applicable to the new messages defined here.

The operation of the procedures does not of itself constitute a security risk because it does not cause any change in network state. It would be possible, if the messages were intercepted or spoofed, to cause bogus alerts in the management plane, so the use of the LMP security measures is RECOMMENDED. Performing the procedures may also provide a useful additional security measure to verify that data channels have not been illicitly modified.
sections.plainLanguage: The exchange changes nothing in the network, so it is safe to run. But a spoofed message could raise a false alarm, so the usual LMP protections are recommended.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA maintains the Link Management Protocol registry, which has a subregistry called LMP Message Type. Three new allocations were made from it: value 32 for ConfirmDataChannelStatus, 33 for ConfirmDataChannelStatusAck and 34 for ConfirmDataChannelStatusNack.

The registry also holds an embedded DATA_LINK sub-object class registry, from which value 9 was allocated for the Data Channel Status subobject. Finally, a new ERROR_CODE class type was allocated, value 4, for the ConfirmDataChannelStatusNack message.
sections.plainLanguage: The three new messages, the new subobject and the new error type were each given a number so that different vendors implement them the same way.

viz.caption: THE DATA CHANNEL STATUS CONFIRMATION EXCHANGE

messages.label: ConfirmDataChannelStatus
messages.note: Carries the local status of one or more data channels and asks for the remote status.

messages.label: ConfirmDataChannelStatusAck
messages.note: Returns the remote end's statuses, whether or not they match.

messages.label: ConfirmDataChannelStatusNack
messages.note: Sent instead of the acknowledgement when the procedure is unsupported or the receiver is unwilling to start it.

items.label: ConfirmDataChannelStatus
items.desc: Reports the local status of one or more data channels and asks for the remote status.

items.label: ConfirmDataChannelStatusAck
items.desc: Returns the requested data channel statuses to the sender.

items.label: ConfirmDataChannelStatusNack
items.desc: Rejects the request, with an error code of 0x01 for unsupported or 0x02 for unwilling.

viz.caption: THE THREE WAYS A DATA CHANNEL GETS STRANDED

items.title: Manual configuration
items.text: An operator cross-connected one end only, so the channel is allocated at one end and still free at the other.

items.title: Interrupted path teardown
items.text: A node resets while an LSP is being deleted, leaving its cross-connect in place while the neighbours remove theirs.

items.title: Failed termination point
items.text: One end sees the termination point as broken and the other sees it as working, so the path setup fails.

items.label: Available
items.desc: The channel is free and can be assigned.

items.label: In use
items.desc: The channel is unavailable, being cross-connected or bound to an end-point.
